name: Periods: what is normal and when to see a GP
summary: The NHS describes a period as lasting 2 to 7 days, every 28 days on average. A GP can help if periods change, hurt or stop.
keyPoints: The NHS says the average cycle is about 28 days, and regular cycles of 21 to 35 days are normal.
A period usually lasts 2 to 7 days, according to the NHS, with an average of 5 days.
The NHS lists periods lasting longer than 7 days and bleeding between periods as reasons to book a GP appointment.
Pain that stops someone doing usual activities, or periods that stop for more than 3 months when not pregnant, are reasons to see a GP.

body.heading: What does a normal period look like?
body.body:
The NHS describes a period as the time in the menstrual cycle when blood and tissue from the womb lining leave the body. The cycle is counted from the first day of one period to the day before the next. If an egg is not fertilised, levels of the hormones oestrogen and progesterone fall, and the womb lining comes away.

The NHS says the average is a period about every 28 days. It says regular cycles that are shorter or longer, from 21 to 35 days, are also normal. A period usually lasts 2 to 7 days, and the average is 5 days. Some other NHS services give wider ranges. NHS 111 Wales gives 21 to 40 days for a regular cycle, and NHS Inform gives around 4 to 8 days for how long a period lasts. The numbers are therefore a guide and not a strict rule.

body.heading: What counts as an irregular period?
body.body:
The NHS says periods are irregular when they come more often than every 21 days or less often than every 35 days. Irregular can also mean a wide change in the gap between periods, in how much blood is lost, or in how many days a period lasts.

The NHS lists several common causes. These include puberty, the approach of menopause, pregnancy, some hormonal contraception, large changes in weight, stress and overexercise. Conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome and thyroid problems can sometimes be the cause. The NHS says treatment is not always needed for irregular periods.

body.heading: When are painful periods a reason to see a GP?
body.body:
The NHS says a GP appointment is advised if periods become more painful, heavier or irregular, or if period pain stops someone doing their usual daily activities. NHS Inform says period pain is usually caused by the womb contracting to push out blood.

The NHS says painful periods can sometimes be linked to conditions such as endometriosis, fibroids or pelvic inflammatory disease. It lists severe period pain that stops normal activities as a symptom of endometriosis, and says a GP is usually the first point of contact and can refer someone to a gynaecologist. If pelvic or period pain is severe, or worse than usual, and painkillers have not helped, the NHS advises calling NHS 111.

body.heading: What if periods stop or are missed?
body.body:
The NHS says common reasons for missed or stopped periods include pregnancy, stress, sudden weight loss, overexercising and reaching the menopause. If periods stop and someone is worried, the NHS says to see a GP.

The NHS advises seeing a GP when someone is not pregnant, has had a negative pregnancy test, and has missed more than 3 periods in a row. It also lists periods that stop before the age of 45 as a reason. A GP may ask about medical history, recent weight changes and how much exercise is taken. NHS Inform says treatment depends on the cause, and a GP may suggest waiting to see whether periods return on their own.

body.heading: What if periods have not started yet?
body.body:
The NHS says to see a GP if periods have not started by the age of 15, or by 13 if there are no other signs of puberty. NHS Inform gives a slightly later age, saying it is a good idea to see a doctor if periods have not started by around 16.

NHS Inform lists several reasons for a late start. These include being underweight, a hormone imbalance, severe stress, an eating disorder, extreme amounts of exercise, pregnancy and a medical condition. It also notes that if a mother or sister started later, others in the family may too.

body.heading: What helps before the appointment, and where do other period problems fit?
body.body:
The NHS says it can help to keep a diary of symptoms across the menstrual cycle before seeing a GP. This gives the doctor a clearer picture of what happens, and when. The NHS also suggests seeing a healthcare professional for fainting during a period, or for needing to stay in bed because of severe pain or heavy bleeding.

Heavy periods have their own guide on this site, which covers causes, tests and treatment. An NHS trust describes irregular and often infrequent periods as typical of polycystic ovary syndrome. NHS Inform describes premenstrual syndrome as mood and physical symptoms in the second half of the cycle, linked to changing hormone levels. The NHS also lists menstrual migraines as a reason to see a GP. Keeping a symptom diary for at least two cycles is suggested by NHS Inform.
